subject: Service-plane separation and traffic policing — evidence pack request

From: Julia Phelps <julia.phelps@greenwave.com>

Cc: security@greenwave.com
Date: Tue, 1 Dec 2026 09:12:00 -0800
Subject: Request: separation boundaries + traffic policing for Dedicated/Private deployment

Hi Karthik,

Thanks for taking this on. As part of our vendor-security review for GreenWave's upcoming Dedicated deployment, we need a concise package that explains how Redwood separates the service/control/data planes between tenants and how you enforce traffic policing at the edges. Specifically we need: 

- A short narrative (1 page) explaining service-plane separation and the controls that enforce it.
- Network diagrams showing L3/L2 boundaries for Private and Dedicated modes.
- Concrete examples of intent-based policies or ACLs you apply for tenant egress (sample rules are fine).
- Any evidence that these controls are tested (runbooks, test artifacts).

Can you provide this by Dec 15? Our compliance team will review and may follow up with a few clarifying questions.

Best,
Julia
Julia Phelps
Security Engineering Manager
GreenWave Health

Julia Phelps
GreenWave Health

Subject: Re: Request: separation boundaries + traffic policing for Dedicated/Private deployment

Julia —

Thanks, we can do that. Attaching a compact evidence pack that covers the items you listed. Highlights:

- service-plane-separation.pdf (attached): 2-page narrative + annotated diagram. Calls out the split between orchestration/control plane (control plane), model-serving plane (service plane), and tenant dataspace.
- traffic-policies.csv: canonical set of sample ACLs we apply on Dedicated edge routers and Private egress gateways.
- network-appendix-v2.drawio: editable diagram with layer labels and interface names.
- egress-acls-sample.txt: example iptables/ACL snippets we run during canary tests.

Quick summary (from the packet):
- Logical separation: each tenant gets isolated compute pools with explicit namespace enforcement; the control plane communicates over authenticated mTLS connections to per-tenant agents that have short-lived certs.
- Traffic policing: per-tenant shaping at the edge (rate limiting + connection caps) plus egress ACLs implemented by cloud VPC firewalls or on-prem routers depending on deployment.
- Fallbacks and fail-open behavior: control plane failures degrade to read-only mode; runtime requests are served from pinned model caches to avoid cross-tenant routing.

We're happy to run a short walkthrough with your team after you've had a look. I copied Laura and Soojin to confirm the technical bits and Vanessa for any contractual notes.

-Karthik
Karthik Iyer
Director, Security & Compliance
Redwood Inference

Julia / team —

Quick technical clarifications on the sample ACLs I attached to the appendix:

- Policy ordering matters: we evaluate deny-list rules first, then per-tenant allow-lists. The CSV contains an explicit order column.
- Egress classification: we tag traffic by service-tag at the NAT gateway so we can apply different policing for observability traffic vs. model scoring traffic.
- Enforcement points: for Redwood Dedicated we push ACLs to the host-edge (VTEP) and cloud provider VPC firewalls; for Private (on-prem) we provide a recommended router config and an Ansible playbook to apply it.

Soojin
